# Quadratic flux, projective deformation, and the mixed moment terms

This note uses the hypotheses and normalized stress certificate of
`candidate d485228e666ca27b`. Its allocation and coincidence conventions
were independently checked in `unshared historical review/context (not an accepted premise)`.
No assertion below is a proof of OC.

## 1. Notation and the exact identity

All positive fibers are compact full-dimensional polytopes in R^d, with d>=1.
Their shared ambient body planes are

    n_f dot x + a_f dot z <= b_f.

Initially each continuous normal n_f is a unit vector. On a facet with several
owners, the objective allocations omega_f sum to one. The cap-body allocations
alpha_jf and effective section measures nu_jz have the consistent meanings in
the audited stress note, including its two coincidence cases. Put

    dW_f = (omega_f - sum_j lambda_j alpha_jf) dH_(d-1),

with the separate traces at different integer indices included in the same
measure. The shared-plane equations are

    integral W_f = 0,
    integral z W_f = 0,
    integral x W_f = 0.                                      (1)

Write the cap planes as v_j dot z + u_j dot x = b_j, with unit u_j. Each
stressed cap j belongs to a positive circuit i. All its effective section
measures have the same full centroid (zbar_i,xbar_i), and

    lambda_j S_j = rho_j t_i,
    sum_(j in i) rho_j (b_j-v_j dot zbar_i) = 0,               (2)

where S_j=sum_z nu_jz(R^d). Define the unnormalized moments

    m   = sum_z integral_(K_z) x dx,
    m_j = sum_z integral_(K_z intersect H_j,z) x dx,
    B_f = integral z tensor x dW_f,
    C_j = sum_z integral (z-zbar_i) tensor (x-xbar_i) dnu_jz.

The tensors B_f and C_j are n-by-d matrices. For a in R^n, the notation
a dot B means the vector in R^d whose k-th coordinate is sum_l a_l B_lk.

**Lemma 1 (mixed quadratic-flux identity).** Under this certificate,

    (d+1)(m-sum_j lambda_j m_j)
      = -sum_f a_f dot B_f -sum_j lambda_j v_j dot C_j.        (3)

In particular, for n=0 the right side vanishes.

**Proof.** Fix h in R^d and use the vector field

    V_h(x)=x(h dot x),      div V_h=(d+1)(h dot x).

Its normal component is identical for all owners of one facet. Consequently
the divergence theorem, and sum omega=1, give

    sum_f integral (n_f dot x)(h dot x) omega_f
      = (d+1) h dot m.                                      (4)

Let t_j(z)=b_j-v_j dot z. On a proper cut section, the outward normal of
K_z intersect H_j,z is -u_j. Its flux is therefore
-t_j(z) integral (h dot x) dH_(d-1). Moving this term to the other side gives

    sum_f integral (n_f dot x)(h dot x) alpha_jf
      = (d+1) h dot m_j
          +sum_z t_j(z) integral (h dot x) dnu_jz.            (5)

This formula also holds with the same allocations at coincident facets.
For a body-inside-cap coincidence n_f=-u_j and sum_f alpha_jf=1-sigma:
removing the sigma portion of the body flux adds sigma t_j(z) times the
section first moment, exactly the term with nu_jz=sigma H_(d-1).
For a body-outside-cap coincidence n_f=u_j and sum_f alpha_jf=sigma:
the cap has zero volume at that fiber and its allocated body flux itself
equals sigma t_j(z) times that first moment. A full or empty noncoincident
cap has no cut-section term. Thus (5) includes every branch without changing
the allocation between its body and section occurrences.

Subtract the lambda-weighted equations (5) from (4). On body plane f,
n_f dot x=b_f-a_f dot z. Equation (1) cancels the b_f first-moment term,
so the result is

    (d+1)(m-sum_j lambda_j m_j)
      = -sum_f a_f dot B_f +sum_j lambda_j sum_z t_j(z) X_jz, (6)

where X_jz=integral x dnu_jz. The common section centroids imply

    sum_z z tensor X_jz = S_j zbar_i tensor xbar_i + C_j.

Hence

    sum_z t_j(z) X_jz
      = S_j(b_j-v_j dot zbar_i)xbar_i - v_j dot C_j.

The lambda-weighted first term vanishes within each group by (2). Substitution
in (6) proves (3). Every measure is finite on compact facet traces, so all
the displayed sums and first and second moments exist. The argument also
applies for d=1, with endpoint H_0 measures and the one-dimensional divergence
theorem. The field V_h was used for a flux identity; it is not asserted to
be an admissible ambient-plane deformation when n>0. QED.

## 2. The continuous consequence and the lost deformation

When n=0, (3) says integral_K x=sum_j lambda_j integral_(K intersect H_j)x.
If M=|K|, every active cap has volume beta M and the homothety normalization
is sum lambda_j=1/beta, this becomes

    centroid(K)=sum_j (beta lambda_j) centroid(K intersect H_j). (7)

Thus the bulk centroid is a convex combination of the cap centroids. This
identity alone does not identify it with the common section centroid.

There is a geometric explanation for the absence of the two terms in (3).
For n=0, the projective map x'=x/(1-t h dot x), on its positive chart for
small t, changes a body plane n_f dot x<=b_f into

    (n_f-t b_f h) dot x' <= b_f.

Its first-order velocity is b_f(h dot x), equal on that plane to the normal
component of V_h. It is an admissible common projective deformation of all
the planes. If the common contact is at zero, it also preserves conical cap
halfspaces through that contact.

For n>0, applying this projective map only in the continuous coordinates
changes the shared plane into

    [n_f-t(b_f-a_f dot z)h] dot x' + a_f dot z <= b_f.

The term (a_f dot z)(h dot x') is bilinear in the ambient variables. It is
not an allowable shared ambient plane. Applying a full ambient projective
map would instead change the integer lattice. Formula (3) records precisely
the extra body and section mixed moments that remain in the fiberwise flux
calculation. Their vanishing is not a consequence of (1) or of the section
centroid equations.

For n=0, the actual positive-circuit caps cover all of R^d. Therefore one
contains the ordinary centroid of K. The ordinary continuous Grunbaum
theorem gives beta>=gamma_d. This is a valid classical recovery of the
constant from the cap cover, but it uses that classical theorem; (7) does
not supply a new proof of it.

The analogous centroid-cover step fails for n>0 already on the sharp product
[0,1] times a simplex K. Let g be the simplex centroid and write its centroid
facet caps as u_j dot (x-g)>=0, with a positive zero-sum circuit of u_j.
For sufficiently large L the groups

    u_j dot (x-g)-Lz>=0,
    u_j dot (x-g)+L(z-1)>=0

cut only their respective integer fibers z=0 and z=1. Each cap has mass
gamma_d |K|, and the groups cover the two integer fibers. At the ordinary
mixed barycenter (1/2,g), every displayed left side equals -L/2. The projected
group halfspaces cover the integer support, but not its convex hull.

## 3. Exact certificates for the missing terms

### 3.1 Signed facet moments do not determine the cross moment

Take n=1,d=2 and the actual convex body over 0<=z<=1 with fibers

    K_z=[-1,1] times [z-1,z].

The upper shared facet has x_2-z=0, so n=(0,1), a=-1, b=0. On its two
integer traces define signed densities w_0(x_1)=x_1 and w_1(x_1)=-x_1.
They are bounded in [-1,1]. Oddness and integral_(-1)^1 x_1^2 dx_1=2/3 give

    integral W=0, integral z W=0, integral x W=(0,0),
    integral z tensor x dW=(-2/3,0).

This certifies that the three moment equations (1), even on genuine shared
facet traces with bounded densities, do not imply B_f=0. It is not claimed
to realize all cap and stress data simultaneously.

### 3.2 A genuine centroidal section has nonzero mixed covariance

Take n=1,d=2 and

    C={|z|<=1, (x_1-z)^2+x_2^2<=1}.

Its three integer fibers are unit disks centered at (z,0). The cut
z/2+x_2=0 through the origin has section lengths sqrt(3),2,sqrt(3).
Their centers are (z,-z/2). The full section centroid is the origin, but

    C_zx=(2 sqrt(3),-sqrt(3)),
    sum_z (-z/2) X_z=(-sqrt(3),sqrt(3)/2).

The mixed set is centrally symmetric, so this cut and its opposite are
depth-minimizing cuts at the origin, of depth one half. Thus a genuine
minimizing centroidal section can have nonzero mixed covariance. The two
opposite cuts cancel in a symmetric summed stress; this example makes no
claim that their total term in (3) is nonzero.

## 4. A tempting mixed-volume closure already fails for n=0

For n=0 and noncoincident cap/body facets, the zeroth facet equations imply,
for every convex body L,

    sum_j lambda_j V((K intersect H_j)[d-1],L)
      = V(K[d-1],L) + (1/d)sum_j lambda_j S_j h_L(-u_j).     (8)

Indeed, the old facet portions on the left have the same weighted area as
each facet of K, while each cap contributes its additional cut facet with
outward normal -u_j and area S_j. This is exactly the polytope formula for
mixed volume; a coincident case would require the effective allocations.

Taking L=K in (8), Minkowski's first inequality and |K intersect H_j|=beta M
give

    beta^(-1/d) M <= M+(1/d)sum_j lambda_j S_j h_K(-u_j).    (9)

An upper bound sum lambda_j S_j h_K(-u_j)<=M would close (9) to
beta>=(d/(d+1))^d. That upper bound is false under the recorded stress
identities, even for a fully realized continuous example.

Let d=2 and K=conv{(1,0),(0,1),(-1,0),(0,-1)}, of area M=2. Use the two
caps H_+={x_1>=0}, H_-={x_1<=0}, lambda_+=lambda_-=1 and rho_+=rho_-=1/2.
Each cap has area one, so beta=1/2 and sum lambda=1/beta. Each section has
length S=2 and centroid zero. Taking the circuit stress t=4 gives
lambda S=rho t. The cap normals sum to zero and their common contact is
zero. On every body facet, except the null intersection with x_1=0, the two
cap indicators partition one. Hence W_f=0 pointwise: every signed zeroth
and first moment equation is satisfied. Nevertheless,

    sum_j lambda_j S_j h_K(-u_j)=2+2=4>M=2.                 (10)

This is a rank-one positive circuit in dimension two. It disproves the
proposed bound from the stress equations as stated, which allow such
circuits; it does not address an additional full-rank hypothesis. Nor does
it assert that this diamond minimizes maximum depth over all convex bodies.
It shows exactly why (8) and the available moments do not close via that
particular upper bound.

All rational arithmetic in Sections 3.1 and 4 is checked in
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_shared_facet_projective_moments.py`; Section 3.2 follows directly
from disk chord lengths and the displayed symmetric centers.
